title: Into your hands (Luke 23:44–56)
hook: Father, into your hands I commend my spirit; the women prepare spices
tomorrow: why seek the living among the dead?

segments.voice: Yesterday, paradise, promised to a dying thief. Your line was they know not what they do. When did you say it before you answered someone? Day five hundred eighty-seven.

Some prayers are learned so early that they're there when nothing else is. A child's bedtime prayer. A line a grandmother said every night. Jesus grew up praying the Psalms, and the line he reaches for at the end comes from Psalm thirty-one. It's around noon now, and Luke says darkness covers the whole land until three in the afternoon. The sun's light fails. In the temple, the curtain of the sanctuary is torn down the middle. And Jesus, who has been praying all through this Gospel, prays one last time, with a line from the prayers of his people.

In the King James words: "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit: and having said thus, he gave up the ghost." Commend means to hand over, to entrust, the way you'd give someone you love into another's care. The psalm says it this way in the King James: "Into thine hand I commit my spirit: thou hast redeemed me, O LORD God of truth." Jesus adds one word to the front of it: Father. In Mark and Matthew, the last cry from the cross is a different psalm, my God, why hast thou forsaken me. Luke gives us this one instead. Christians hold both, and hear in them two sides of the same death: real abandonment, and real trust. Then Luke turns to the people watching. A Roman centurion, who has seen executions before, glorifies God and says, "Certainly this was a righteous man." The crowds go home beating their breasts. His friends, and the women who had followed him from Galilee, stand at a distance and watch. Then a man named Joseph, from Arimathea, steps forward. He's a member of the council, and Luke tells us he hadn't agreed with their decision. He asks Pilate for the body, wraps it in linen, and lays it in a tomb cut into rock, where no one had ever been laid. The women follow and see where. They go home and prepare spices and ointments. And then, Luke says, they rested on the sabbath, according to the commandment. Even in the worst grief, they keep the sabbath, and wait.
screen: then, large: `INTO THY HANDS I COMMEND MY SPIRIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say the words before sleep. You can begin now. Settle, and breathe. Think of what you'll carry into bed tonight: your body, tired; your worries; the people you love. Imagine opening your hands and placing each one into hands larger than yours. You don't have to know how it will turn out. If you pray, you can say it, now and tonight before sleep: into thy hands I commend my spirit. If you don't, simply open your hands on your lap and let the day go. The bell holds the time.
Into your hands. Jesus's last words from the cross in Luke, from Psalm thirty-one: a child's prayer of trust, spoken at the end.
Your line: into your hands. Tonight, before you sleep, open your hands and say the line, and let the day go. Day five hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Christians in many traditions pray 'into thy hands' at night prayer, Compline, as the day ends, and on Good Friday the last words from the cross are read and remembered.

myth: Jesus's last words are the same in every Gospel
in Mark and Matthew he cries 'why hast thou forsaken me'; in Luke, 'into thy hands I commend my spirit'.
Joseph of Arimathea was a member of the council
Luke says he had not consented to their counsel and deed.
the women rested on the sabbath before going to the tomb
they rested the sabbath day according to the commandment.

fork.setup: you're Joseph of Arimathea, a council member who disagreed with its decision. Jesus is dead, and the sabbath is near. what do you do?
options: ask Pilate for the body and lay it in a new tomb.
denounce the council in the street.
fork.reveal: he goes to Pilate, begs the body, wraps it in linen, and lays it in a rock tomb where no one had ever been laid.

original.note: Greek: I entrust, I hand over into someone's keeping. Luke's word for 'I commend'.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus's last words, said as he died.
what it means: a line of trust from Psalm 31, with 'Father' added, handing his life into God's keeping.
what a scholar hears: Luke's last word differs from Mark's 'why hast thou forsaken me', and the psalm line later became part of Christian night prayer, Compline.

notes: The hook says Jesus grew up praying the Psalms (an inference from his frequent use of them in the Gospels). Later Jewish night prayer includes Psalm 31:6 (Hebrew numbering); first-century usage is uncertain, so the script doesn't claim it.
Sixth to ninth hour rendered as noon to three. Confirm.
Joseph 'had not consented to the counsel and deed of them' (Luke 23:51). Confirm.
Compline use of 'Into your hands' (In manus tuas) as the responsory. Confirm.
